title: Τὸ σῆμα τῶν αἰετῶν
titleEn: The Sign of the Eagles — Odyssey 2.103–207
about: Continuing directly from Antinous's account of how the suitors caught Penelope unweaving her web by night, Telemachus refuses to send his mother from the house and calls on the gods for a reckoning against the men consuming his estate. Zeus then sends a pair of eagles wheeling in a portent over the assembly, and the old seer Halitherses reads it as a sign that Odysseus is near and that ruin awaits the suitors. Eurymachus answers with contempt, dismissing the prophecy, threatening Halitherses with a fine, and vowing that the suitors will not give up their courtship of Penelope — his defiant speech still running as the part ends.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, ἡμῖν δ’ αὖτ’ ἐπεπείθετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and then our own lordly heart was persuaded;
sentences.i: So she said, and our own proud hearts were won over.
sentences.n: This unit continues Antinous's speech from the previous part with no new opening quotation mark and no mark field, since the speech and its mark were already given there; ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο, the imperfect middle of φημί, closing the report of Penelope's own promise. ἐπεπείθετο, built on the perfect stem of πείθω with the augment, functions here as a plain imperfect, 'was won over'. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ uses the same adjective already fixed as 'lordly' in the house table's μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες, here applied to the suitors' own hearts rather than to the suitors themselves.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα καὶ ἠματίη μὲν ὑφαίνεσκεν μέγαν ἱστόν,
νύκτας δ’ ἀλλύεσκεν, ἐπεὶ δαΐδας παραθεῖτο.
sentences.l:
There by day she would weave the great web,
but by nights she would unravel it, when she had set torches beside her.
sentences.i: There by day she would weave her great web, and by night unravel it again, once she had placed torches beside her.
sentences.n: ὑφαίνεσκεν and ἀλλύεσκεν are iterative imperfects in -σκον, marking repeated or habitual past action ('she would weave... she would unravel'); this iterative formation recurs through this account of the ruse. δαΐδας παραθεῖτο is an aorist optative in a clause of repeated circumstance, 'whenever she had set out torches', an idiom that pairs with the -σκον verbs. δαΐδας 'torches' is the same noun as in the house table's αἰθομένας δαΐδας φέρε.

sentences.t: ὣς τρίετες μὲν ἔληθε δόλῳ καὶ ἔπειθεν Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.l: So for three years, by her trick, she escaped notice and deceived the Achaeans;
sentences.i: So for three years her trick went undetected, and she deceived the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἔληθε is the imperfect of the epic simplex λήθω (a poetic by-form of λανθάνω), regularly augmented (ἐ-ληθε), 'was escaping notice'; ἔπειθεν is likewise a normally augmented imperfect of πείθω (ἐ-πειθε(ν)) — neither shows the augment-dropping this poem notes elsewhere. λήθω/λανθάνω with a dative of means, δόλῳ, is 'escape notice by means of a trick'; τρίετες is an adverbial accusative of duration, 'for three years'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε τέτρατον ἦλθεν ἔτος καὶ ἐπήλυθον ὧραι,
καὶ τότε δή τις ἔειπε γυναικῶν, ἣ σάφα ᾔδη,
καὶ τήν γ’ ἀλλύουσαν ἐφεύρομεν ἀγλαὸν ἱστόν.
sentences.l:
But when the fourth year came, and the seasons passed by,
then indeed one of the women spoke, one who knew it clearly,
and we caught her, in the act, undoing the splendid web.
sentences.i: But when the fourth year came round and the seasons had passed, one of the women, who knew the truth of it, spoke out, and we caught her undoing the splendid web.
sentences.n: ἐπήλυθον is an unaugmented aorist of ἐπέρχομαι (Attic ἐπῆλθον). ὧραι is 'the seasons, the year's round'. ἔειπε is an epic aorist 'spoke, said', built on the same root as the more familiar εἶπε; ἐφεύρομεν is a first-person plural aorist, 'we found/caught her', Antinous speaking throughout for the suitors as a body. ἀγλαόν 'splendid, radiant' varies μέγαν of line 104 for the same web.

sentences.t: ὣς τὸ μὲν ἐξετέλεσσε καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλουσ’ ὑπ’ ἀνάγκης·
sentences.l: So that she finished, even unwilling, under compulsion;
sentences.i: So she finished the web, against her will, under compulsion.
sentences.n: τό is the pronoun again rather than the article, 'it', referring back to the web ἱστόν — a pattern to expect constantly in Homer. ἐξετέλεσσε is the aorist of ἐκτελέω 'bring to completion'; ἐθέλουσα is a participle agreeing with the unexpressed subject Penelope, concessive in force ('though unwilling') despite lacking περ.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ ὧδε μνηστῆρες ὑποκρίνονται, ἵν’ εἰδῇς
αὐτὸς σῷ θυμῷ, εἰδῶσι δὲ πάντες Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.l:
So to you the suitors answer thus, that you yourself
may know it in your own heart, and all the Achaeans may know it;
sentences.i: This, then, is the suitors' answer to you, so that you yourself may know it in your own heart, and all the Achaeans may know it too.
sentences.n: σῷ is the possessive adjective ὅς, ἥ, ὅν, 'his, her, your own', not to be confused with the identically-spelled relative pronoun; here 'in your own heart'. Antinous now turns from narrating Penelope's ruse to address Telemachus directly. ἵν’ εἰδῇς and εἰδῶσι are subjunctives in a purpose clause with ἵνα, from οἶδα.

sentences.t:
μητέρα σὴν ἀπόπεμψον, ἄνωχθι δέ μιν γαμέεσθαι
τῷ ὅτεῴ τε πατὴρ κέλεται καὶ ἁνδάνει αὐτῇ.
sentences.l:
Send your mother away, and bid her be married
to whomever her father commands, and who is pleasing to her.
sentences.i: Send your mother back to her father's house, and tell her to marry whomever her father chooses and she herself is pleased with.
sentences.n: ἄνωχθι is the perfect imperative of the defective verb ἄνωγα 'command', used with present force; it recurs at 2.195 as ἀνωγέτω. ὅτεῳ is the epic dative of the indefinite ὅστις (Attic ὅτῳ), and τε here marks the clause as a general, standing condition, 'to whomever'; this is the 'epic τε' that marks a general truth rather than a simple connective. γαμέεσθαι, uncontracted, is the middle infinitive used of the woman, 'be given in marriage', distinct from the active used of the man.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἔτ’ ἀνιήσει γε πολὺν χρόνον υἷας Ἀχαιῶν,
τὰ φρονέουσ’ ἀνὰ θυμόν, ὅ οἱ πέρι δῶκεν Ἀθήνη
ἔργα τ’ ἐπίστασθαι περικαλλέα καὶ φρένας ἐσθλὰς
κέρδεά θ’, οἷ’ οὔ πώ τιν’ ἀκούομεν οὐδὲ παλαιῶν,
sentences.l:
But if she will go on vexing the sons of the Achaeans for a long time yet,
pondering in her heart these things, which beyond others Athena gave her—
to know very-beautiful works, and a noble mind,
and cunning-ways, such as we have not yet heard of, not even among women of old,
sentences.i: But if she goes on distressing the sons of the Achaeans for much longer, turning over in her heart what Athena has given her beyond other women — skill in very beautiful handiwork, a noble mind, and cunning ways such as we have never heard of, not even among the women of old,
sentences.n: υἷας Ἀχαιῶν, 'sons of the Achaeans', is a fixed periphrasis for the young Achaean men — here the suitors themselves — kept the same wherever it recurs (see new-renderings.md). πέρι after ὅ οἱ is adverbial, 'exceedingly, beyond others', with its accent thrown back (anastrophe), as with φίλων ἄπο in the pilot. ἔργα ἐπίστασθαι ... κέρδεά θ’ lists, by epexegetic infinitives, the gifts Athena gave Penelope: skill in fine handiwork, a noble mind, and κέρδεα 'cunning-ways', a positive shrewdness here rather than trickery. This unit is cut at a comma, short of a full stop, because the sentence that runs from 2.115 would otherwise span six lines; the clause continues in the next unit.

sentences.t:
τάων αἳ πάρος ἦσαν ἐυπλοκαμῖδες Ἀχαιαί,
Τυρώ τ’ Ἀλκμήνη τε ἐυστέφανός τε Μυκήνη·
sentences.l:
of those who formerly were the fair-tressed Achaean women,
Tyro, and Alcmene, and fair-crowned Mycene;
sentences.i: among the fair-tressed Achaean women of the past — Tyro, and Alcmene, and fair-crowned Mycene;
sentences.n: ἐυπλοκαμῖδες, literally 'women of the fine locks', is a distinct nominal formation from the adjective ἐυπλόκαμος, already used of the nymph Calypso at 1.86 ('fine-plaited' in the pilot's own draft, though not itself a recurring house-table entry); its own rendering is fixed in new-renderings.md. Tyro, Alcmene (mother of Heracles) and Mycene, eponym of the city, are named as the great heroines of the heroic past — the standard against which Antinous ironically measures Penelope's cunning. ἐυστέφανος 'fair-crowned' is likewise fixed in new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
τάων οὔ τις ὁμοῖα νοήματα Πηνελοπείῃ
ᾔδη·
sentences.l:
of these, none — thoughts like Penelope's —
knew;
sentences.i: none of them knew designs to match Penelope's;
sentences.n: τάων is the pronoun again, 'of these women'. νόημα 'thought, design' is from νοέω; Πηνελοπείῃ is a dative of comparison. ἴδη is the pluperfect of οἶδα used with imperfect force, 'knew' — the same form as σάφα ἴδη of line 108.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ μὲν τοῦτό γ’ ἐναίσιμον οὐκ ἐνόησε.
sentences.l: yet in this thing, at least, she devised nothing fitting.
sentences.i: but in this one thing she did not act as she should have.
sentences.n: ἐναίσιμος, 'in due measure, fitting', is built on αἶσα 'a due share, portion'. Antinous turns here from grudging praise of Penelope's cleverness to blame: however clever the scheme, it was not, he says, a fitting thing to do. ἐνόησε answers νοήματα in the line before.

sentences.t:
τόφρα γὰρ οὖν βίοτόν τε τεὸν καὶ κτήματ’ ἔδονται,
ὄφρα κε κείνη τοῦτον ἔχῃ νόον, ὅν τινά οἱ νῦν
ἐν στήθεσσι τιθεῖσι θεοί.
sentences.i: for just as long as they will go on eating up your living and your goods, so long will she keep the purpose that the gods are now placing in her heart.
sentences.n: τεόν is the epic possessive 'your' (= σόν). ἔδονται is the ordinary Homeric future of ἐσθίω, middle in form. τόφρα ... ὄφρα κε is a correlative pair, 'for exactly as long as'. στήθεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, plural for a single chest, the same body-part plural pattern as σπέσσι in the pilot's opening.

sentences.t:
μέγα μὲν κλέος αὐτῇ
ποιεῖτ’, αὐτὰρ σοί γε ποθὴν πολέος βιότοιο.
sentences.l:
great fame for herself
she wins, but for you, at least, the want of much substance.
sentences.i: great fame she is winning for herself, but for you it means the loss of a great livelihood.
sentences.n: κλέος 'fame' was fixed as 'good fame' with ἐσθλόν in the house table; here it stands with μέγα 'great' instead, and 'fame' is kept as the noun to match. ποθή, 'a missing, a want of', takes the genitive of the thing lacked, πολέος βιότοιο, a genitive singular in -οιο (Attic -ου), the epic ending already met in the pilot.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ οὔτ’ ἐπὶ ἔργα πάρος γ’ ἴμεν οὔτε πῃ ἄλλῃ,
πρίν γ’ αὐτὴν γήμασθαι Ἀχαιῶν ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλῃσι.
sentences.l:
But we will not go, before then, to our own work, nor anywhere else,
until she herself is married to whichever of the Achaeans she wishes.”
sentences.i: And we will not go off to our own affairs, or anywhere else, until she marries whichever of the Achaeans she pleases.”
sentences.n: This unit closes Antinous's speech, which began in the previous part and has run without a break through this whole stretch; the closing ” belongs here, on the last unit before the reply-formula at 2.129. ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλῃσι uses κε with the subjunctive for a general 'whichever she may wish', the epic equivalent of ἄν. γήμασθαι, the same middle infinitive as γαμέεσθαι at 2.113, is used again of the woman.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This whole line reuses, verbatim, its earlier appearance in odyssey-004 (1.388): the fixed reply-formula for Telemachus, name and πεπνυμένος 'prudent' and ἀντίον ηὔδα 'spoke face to face'. As narration it carries no mark and no quotation mark of its own; both begin with the next unit, the first words actually spoken.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνο’, οὔ πως ἔστι δόμων ἀέκουσαν ἀπῶσαι
ἥ μ’ ἔτεχ’, ἥ μ’ ἔθρεψε·
sentences.l:
“Antinous, in no way is it possible to drive from the house,
against her will, the woman who bore me, who reared me;
sentences.i: “Antinous, there is no way I can drive from the house, against her will, the woman who bore me and reared me;
sentences.n: This unit opens Telemachus's speech, with the mark and the quotation mark placed here rather than on the reply-formula line, as is done throughout this part. ἔτεχ’ is ἔτεκε, an aorist of τίκτω with the regular augment ἐ- (elided and aspirated to χ before the rough breathing of the next word). ἀέκουσαν is the feminine accusative participle-adjective 'unwilling', anticipating the object of ἀπῶσαι. The two relative clauses, 'who bore me, who reared me', give the two grounds — birth and nurture — for a son's duty to his mother.

sentences.t:
πατὴρ δ’ ἐμὸς ἄλλοθι γαίης,
ζώει ὅ γ’ ἦ τέθνηκε·
sentences.l:
and my father is elsewhere on earth —
whether he lives, or is dead —
sentences.i: while my father is somewhere else in the world, alive or dead, I do not know;
sentences.n: ἄλλοθι γαίης, 'elsewhere of earth', takes a partitive genitive with the adverb, the same construction as ἁμόθεν γε in the pilot's proem; γαίης shows the Ionic η where Attic keeps long α (γαῖα). ζώει ὅ γ’ ἢ τέθνηκε leaves the alternative open, without a governing verb of knowing; 'I do not know' is implicit in the construction.

sentences.t:
κακὸν δέ με πόλλ’ ἀποτίνειν
Ἰκαρίῳ, αἴ κ’ αὐτὸς ἑκὼν ἀπὸ μητέρα πέμψω.
sentences.l:
and it is an evil thing for me to pay back much
to Icarius, if of my own will I send my mother away.
sentences.i: and it would be a heavy thing for me to repay Icarius, if I send my mother away of my own accord.
sentences.n: ἀποτίνειν looks ahead to the bride-gifts that would have to be paid back to Icarius, Penelope's father, if Telemachus himself sent her away rather than her remarrying by her own or the suitors' choice. ἀπὸ ... πέμψω is tmesis: the preverb ἀπό stands apart from its verb (= ἀποπέμψω 'send away'), the same Homeric freedom of word order already noted for κατά … ἤσθιον at 1.8–9 in the pilot. αἴ κ’ is the epic equivalent of ἐάν, with a subjunctive.

sentences.t:
ἐκ γὰρ τοῦ πατρὸς κακὰ πείσομαι, ἄλλα δὲ δαίμων
δώσει, ἐπεὶ μήτηρ στυγερὰς ἀρήσετ’ ἐρινῦς
οἴκου ἀπερχομένη·
sentences.i: for from her father I shall have evils to suffer, and a god will send others besides, since my mother, as she leaves this house, will call down the hateful Furies on me;
sentences.n: πείσομαι is the future of πάσχω 'suffer' (not of πείθω). δαίμων here is vague, 'some god, a divine power'. The Erinyes (Furies) avenge wrongs done to blood-kin, above all a curse spoken by a parent against a child; Telemachus fears such a curse if he expels his mother against her will. ἀρήσετ’ is ἀρήσετο, future of ἀράομαι 'pray for, call down'. οἴκου ἀπερχομένη is a genitive of separation with the participle, 'leaving the house'.

sentences.t:
νέμεσις δέ μοι ἐξ ἀνθρώπων
ἔσσεται·
sentences.l:
and reproach from men
there will be for me;
sentences.i: and I shall have the blame of men besides;
sentences.n: νέμεσις is the disapproval a community turns on someone who has broken a norm; Telemachus fears public blame as well as a private curse if he expels his mother against her wish. ἔσσεται is the uncontracted future of εἰμί (= ἔσται).

sentences.t: ὣς οὐ τοῦτον ἐγώ ποτε μῦθον ἐνίψω.
sentences.l: so this word I will never utter.
sentences.i: so I will never say the word that would send her away.
sentences.n: ἐνίψω is here the future of ἐνέπω 'say, tell' (the same verb as ἔννεπε at the poem's opening), needed as a transitive verb with μῦθον as its object, rather than of ἐνίπτω 'rebuke'. τοῦτον ... μῦθον, 'this word', is the command to expel Penelope that Antinous has just urged. Telemachus now turns, with the conditional clause that opens the next unit, from his mother's case to address the suitors themselves.

sentences.t:
ὑμέτερος δ’ εἰ μὲν θυμὸς νεμεσίζεται αὐτῶν,
ἔξιτέ μοι μεγάρων, ἄλλας δ’ ἀλεγύνετε δαῖτας
ὑμὰ κτήματ’ ἔδοντες ἀμειβόμενοι κατὰ οἴκους.
sentences.l:
But if your own heart feels shame at these things,
then get out of my halls, and see to other feasts,
eating your own possessions, taking turns through your houses.
sentences.i: But if your own hearts feel any shame at this, then get out of my halls, and go and hold your feasts elsewhere, eating up what is your own, moving from house to house in turn.
sentences.n: νεμεσίζεται, built on the same root as νέμεσις two lines above, is 'feels indignation, is ashamed', with αὐτῶν a genitive of the thing felt shame at, their own conduct. μεγάρων is a genitive of separation with ἔξιτε. The wording of ἄλλας δ’ ἀλεγύνετε δαῖτας … κατὰ οἴκους repeats the line already fixed at its first appearance (1.374, odyssey-004), reused here as far as this unit's own boundaries allow.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ὑμῖν δοκέει τόδε λωίτερον καὶ ἄμεινον
ἔμμεναι, ἀνδρὸς ἑνὸς βίοτον νήποινον ὀλέσθαι,
κείρετ’·
sentences.i: But if it seems to you more profitable and better to waste one man’s living without paying for it, then go on and devour it;
sentences.n: This unit reuses, verbatim, its earlier appearance in odyssey-004 (1.376). ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί. νήποινον, 'without requital, unpunished', looks ahead to the vengeance Telemachus threatens in the unit that follows.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δὲ θεοὺς ἐπιβώσομαι αἰὲν ἐόντας,
αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς δῷσι παλίντιτα ἔργα γενέσθαι.
sentences.l:
but I will call upon the gods who are forever,
if somehow Zeus may grant that deeds requited-in-turn come to pass;
sentences.i: but I will call upon the gods who are forever, in hope that Zeus may somehow grant that there be a reckoning for what you have done;
sentences.n: This unit reuses, in wording, its earlier appearance in odyssey-004 (1.378); the Greek there closes with an ano teleia where the present packet has a full stop, but the content is identical. θεοὺς ... αἰὲν ἐόντας is the house formula 'the gods who are forever'. παλίντιτα ἔργα, literally 'deeds paid back again', is a reckoning in kind for what has been done.

sentences.t: νήποινοί κεν ἔπειτα δόμων ἔντοσθεν ὄλοισθε.
sentences.l: then unavenged, within the house, may you all perish.”
sentences.i: then may you all perish inside this house, unavenged.”
sentences.n: This unit reuses, verbatim, its earlier appearance in odyssey-004 (1.380); as there, it closes a speech — here, Telemachus's reply to Antinous. ὄλοισθε is a 2nd plural aorist optative of wish, 'may you perish'.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο Τηλέμαχος, τῷ δ’ αἰετὼ εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
ὑψόθεν ἐκ κορυφῆς ὄρεος προέηκε πέτεσθαι.
sentences.l:
So spoke Telemachus, and for him far-thundering Zeus
from on high, from a mountain peak, sent forth two eagles to fly.
sentences.i: So Telemachus spoke, and for him far-thundering Zeus sent two eagles flying down from a mountain peak on high.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the fixed formula that closes a speech, as already twice in the previous part (2.35, 2.80); here it does double duty, closing Telemachus's speech and opening this new paragraph on Zeus's sign. αἰετώ is a dual, 'the pair of eagles', and the dual number continues through the whole scene (ἐπέτοντο, τιναξάσθην, and so on) until the birds' final flight. ὑψόθεν carries the suffix -θεν 'from', as ἁμόθεν did in the pilot. εὐρύοπα is a nominative in short -α, like νεφεληγερέτα in the house table; its literal sense is disputed and its rendering is fixed in new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἕως μέν ῥ’ ἐπέτοντο μετὰ πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο
πλησίω ἀλλήλοισι τιταινομένω πτερύγεσσιν·
sentences.l:
and the two of them, for a while, flew on amid the blasts of the wind,
close to one another, straining with their wings;
sentences.i: and for a while the two flew on together on the gusts of the wind, close beside each other, their wings straining;
sentences.n: This whole unit is in the dual number (τώ, ἐπέτοντο, πλησίω, τιταινομένω), the number Homer keeps for a natural pair. ῥ’ is a weak, enclitic form of ἄρα, adding a note of natural sequence to the narrative. πνοιῇς and πτερύγεσσιν are datives plural in -ησι/-εσσι, instrumental, as noted at 2.125.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ μέσσην ἀγορὴν πολύφημον ἱκέσθην,
ἔνθ’ ἐπιδινηθέντε τιναξάσθην πτερὰ πυκνά,
ἐς δ’ ἰδέτην πάντων κεφαλάς, ὄσσοντο δ’ ὄλεθρον·
sentences.i: But when they reached the middle of the assembly place, loud with the many voices of the crowd, there they wheeled about and shook out their close feathers, and looked into the faces of everyone, foreboding death;
sentences.n: πολύφημον, 'many-voiced', describes the crowded assembly itself, not the birds. ὄσσομαι, 'have a premonition of, forebode', is a rare Homeric verb, here taking ὄλεθρον as its object; the birds' behaviour is itself read as a portent even before Halitherses puts it into words. ἐς δ’ ἰδέτην is tmesis for ἐσιδέτην, the preverb standing apart from its verb. All the verbs remain dual, continuing the pattern of the previous unit.

sentences.t:
δρυψαμένω δ’ ὀνύχεσσι παρειὰς ἀμφί τε δειρὰς
δεξιὼ ἤιξαν διά τ’ οἰκία καὶ πόλιν αὐτῶν.
sentences.l:
and having torn with their talons cheeks and necks about each other,
they darted away on the right, through the houses and the city of the people.
sentences.i: and after tearing at each other's cheeks and necks with their talons, they sped off to the right, over the houses and the city of the people.
sentences.n: δεξιός 'on the right hand' marks a favourable omen in Greek bird-augury; a sign appearing on the right, facing north, was auspicious. ὀνύχεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, instrumental, 'with their talons', as with the datives noted at 2.125. ἤιξαν shifts to a plural verb, easing away from the dual forms of the last two units even while the eagles still act as a pair. οἰκία καὶ πόλιν αὐτῶν, 'the houses and city of them', means the Ithacans watching below.

sentences.t: θάμβησαν δ’ ὄρνιθας, ἐπεὶ ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσιν·
sentences.l: And they marveled at the birds, when they saw them with their eyes;
sentences.i: And the people were amazed at the birds, when they saw them with their own eyes;
sentences.n: The subject shifts here, without being named, from the eagles to the watching Ithacans in the assembly. ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is another dative plural in -οισι, instrumental, 'with their eyes' — emphatic, since witnessing a sign with one's own eyes carried more weight than hearing of it.

sentences.t: ὥρμηναν δ’ ἀνὰ θυμὸν ἅ περ τελέεσθαι ἔμελλον.
sentences.l: and they turned over in their hearts what things were about to be fulfilled.
sentences.i: and they wondered in their hearts what these signs were going to bring to pass.
sentences.n: ὥρμηναν is the aorist of ὁρμαίνω 'turn over in the mind, ponder', regularly used of weighing a puzzling sign. ἅ περ joins the relative ἅ with the emphatic particle περ, 'what things indeed'; τελέεσθαι is the uncontracted present passive infinitive of τελέω. This unit closes the narrated omen and opens the way for Halitherses' interpretation of it.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε γέρων ἥρως Ἁλιθέρσης
Μαστορίδης·
sentences.l:
And among them spoke also the old hero Halitherses,
son of Mastor;
sentences.i: And among them the old hero Halitherses, son of Mastor, spoke up as well;
sentences.n: μετέειπε, 'spoke among them', is half of the fixed formula ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε that closes at 2.160; here it stands alone to introduce Halitherses himself before his qualifications are given. γέρων 'old' and ἥρως 'the hero' (fixed in the house table as 'the hero') both describe him; Μαστορίδης is a patronymic in -ίδης, 'son of Mastor'.

sentences.t:
ὁ γὰρ οἶος ὁμηλικίην ἐκέκαστο
ὄρνιθας γνῶναι καὶ ἐναίσιμα μυθήσασθαι·
sentences.l:
for he alone, of his own generation, excelled
in knowing birds and speaking forth what was fitting;
sentences.i: for he alone among his contemporaries excelled at reading the birds and declaring what was fated;
sentences.n: ἐκέκαστο is the pluperfect of καίνυμαι 'excel, surpass', used with imperfect force like ᾔδη above; it governs the two infinitives ὄρνιθας γνῶναι and μυθήσασθαι as the respects in which he excelled. Bird-augury — reading the flight and behaviour of birds as a sign of the gods' will — is an old and respected skill in Homer; ἐναίσιμα, 'things in accordance with what is due', are the true portents such skill can discern.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐὺ φρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε·
sentences.l: he, thinking well toward them, addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with good will toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε is the fixed formula for a speaker addressing the assembly, kept the same wording each time it recurs. ἐὺ φρονέων, 'thinking well, well disposed', echoes ἀγαθὰ φρονέων used of Hermes in the pilot. This line is narration; the quoted speech itself, and Halitherses' mark, begin with the next unit.

sentences.t: κέκλυτε δὴ νῦν μευ, Ἰθακήσιοι, ὅττι κεν εἴπω·
sentences.l: “Hear me now, men of Ithaca, whatever I may say;
sentences.i: “Hear me now, men of Ithaca, and hear what I have to say.
sentences.n: This line reuses, verbatim, its earlier appearance in the previous part (2.25), where it opened Aegyptius's speech calling the assembly to attention: the same fixed formula of address, kept to the same wording here in Halitherses' mouth. The opening “ begins his speech.

sentences.t: μνηστῆρσιν δὲ μάλιστα πιφαυσκόμενος τάδε εἴρω·
sentences.l: and to the suitors most of all, declaring it, these things I say;
sentences.i: and it is to the suitors above all that I say this, and make it known to them;
sentences.n: πιφαύσκομαι, 'declare, make plain', is a reduplicated present rare outside Homer. εἴρω here is the verb 'say, tell' (identical in form to some futures), not the verb 'ask'. Halitherses names his true audience before he speaks further.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν γὰρ μέγα πῆμα κυλίνδεται·
sentences.l: for upon them a great woe is rolling;
sentences.i: for a great disaster is rolling down upon them;
sentences.n: κυλίνδεται, literally 'rolls', pictures disaster as an advancing wave or boulder set in motion — a common Homeric image for approaching ruin.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
δὴν ἀπάνευθε φίλων ὧν ἔσσεται, ἀλλά που ἤδη
ἐγγὺς ἐὼν τοῖσδεσσι φόνον καὶ κῆρα φυτεύει
πάντεσσιν·
sentences.i: for Odysseus will not be far from his own people for long; already, somewhere close by, he is sowing death and doom for all of these men;
sentences.n: φυτεύει, literally 'plants, begets', is used metaphorically of setting a disaster in motion, as one plants a seed that will grow. τοῖσδεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι of the demonstrative ὅδε, pointing directly at the suitors present; πάντεσσιν is another such dative. ὧν is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν again, 'his own [dear ones]'.

sentences.t:
πολέσιν δὲ καὶ ἄλλοισιν κακὸν ἔσται,
οἳ νεμόμεσθ’ Ἰθάκην ἐυδείελον.
sentences.l:
and for many others too there will be evil,
we who dwell in clear-seen Ithaca.
sentences.i: and evil will come to many others too, to all of us who live in clear-seen Ithaca.
sentences.n: νεμόμεσθ’ is first person plural present (Attic νεμόμεθα), Halitherses speaking as one of the Ithacans himself. πολέσιν is the dative plural of πολύς (Attic πολλοῖς). ἐυδείελος, a stock epithet of Ithaca whose exact sense is disputed, is fixed in new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρὶν
φραζώμεσθ’, ὥς κεν καταπαύσομεν·
sentences.l:
but well before then
let us take thought, how we may put a stop to it;
sentences.i: but long before that let us take counsel, and see how we can put a stop to it;
sentences.n: φραζώμεσθ’ is a hortatory subjunctive, 'let us consider'; καταπαύσομεν, a future indicative, stands with κεν in a clause of purpose, an idiom found beside the more usual subjunctive. Halitherses turns here from warning to urging action.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ
παυέσθων·
sentences.l:
and let them, too, themselves
stop;
sentences.i: and let them themselves stop too;
sentences.n: παυέσθων is a third-person plural imperative, 'let them stop', addressed to the suitors indirectly through the assembly: Halitherses calls on the suitors to desist of their own accord, alongside the Ithacans' own resolve to act.

sentences.t: καὶ γάρ σφιν ἄφαρ τόδε λώιόν ἐστιν.
sentences.l: for indeed this is at once the better thing for them.
sentences.i: for this course will at once be the better one for them.
sentences.n: λώιον is the comparative of the adjective seen in the house formula τόδε λωίτερον καὶ ἄμεινον at 2.141; Halitherses argues it is in the suitors' own interest to stop, not merely a matter of justice.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἀπείρητος μαντεύομαι, ἀλλ’ ἐὺ εἰδώς·
sentences.l: for I do not prophesy without experience, but knowing it well;
sentences.i: for I do not speak as a prophet without experience, but as one who knows well;
sentences.n: ἀπείρητος, 'untried, inexperienced', is built on the same root as πεῖρα 'trial, experiment'. Halitherses claims the authority of a proven record for what he is about to say, and offers the proof in the unit that follows.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ κείνῳ φημὶ τελευτηθῆναι ἅπαντα,
ὥς οἱ ἐμυθεόμην, ὅτε Ἴλιον εἰσανέβαινον
Ἀργεῖοι, μετὰ δέ σφιν ἔβη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.i: for I tell you that for that man too everything has come to pass just as I told him it would, when the Argives were marching up against Ilios, and Odysseus of many wiles went with them.
sentences.n: τελευτηθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of τελευτάω, in indirect statement after φημί. ἐμυθεόμην is an imperfect, 'I used to tell him'. εἰσανέβαινον is an unaugmented imperfect, 'were going up' — inland, toward the citadel, from the ships on the shore. Ἀργεῖοι, 'the Argives', is one of Homer's three names for the Greeks, alongside Ἀχαιοί and Δαναοί. πολύμητις, 'of many wiles', is an epithet built on μῆτις 'cunning intelligence, craft', kept distinct in both layers from the -φρων epithets (built on φρήν 'mind') and from πολυμήχανος (built on μηχανή 'device'), already fixed in the house table; its rendering is fixed in new-renderings.md, and the l-layer 'many-wiled' (rather than 'many-counselled') keeps it clear of πολύφρων's own i-rendering 'of the many counsels'.

sentences.t:
φῆν κακὰ πολλὰ παθόντ’, ὀλέσαντ’ ἄπο πάντας ἑταίρους,
ἄγνωστον πάντεσσιν ἐεικοστῷ ἐνιαυτῷ
οἴκαδ’ ἐλεύσεσθαι·
sentences.i: I told him that after suffering many evils, and losing all his companions, he would come home unrecognized by everyone, in the twentieth year;
sentences.n: φῆν is the uncontracted first singular imperfect of φημί (= ἔφην), resuming ὡς οἱ ἐμυθεόμην with the content of the old prophecy itself, now in indirect statement with accusative and infinitive (παθόντα, ὀλέσαντα … ἐλεύσεσθαι). ἄπο … ὀλέσαντ’ is tmesis for ἀπολέσαντα. The twenty years are the ten of the war and the ten of the wandering home, the poem's own reckoning of Odysseus's absence.

sentences.t: τὰ δὲ δὴ νῦν πάντα τελεῖται.
sentences.l: and now indeed all these things are being fulfilled.”
sentences.i: and now, indeed, all of it is coming to pass.”
sentences.n: τελεῖται, present passive of τελέω, answers τελευτηθῆναι above and τελέεσθαι at 2.156, tying the eagle-sign, Halitherses' old prophecy, and its fulfilment now into a single thread of vocabulary. This closes Halitherses' speech, which opened at 2.161, and the ” is placed at its end.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Εὐρύμαχος Πολύβου πάϊς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: Him then in turn spoke Eurymachus, Polybus’ son, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Eurymachus, son of Polybus, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This line reuses, verbatim, its earlier appearance in odyssey-004 (1.399): the fixed reply-formula for Eurymachus, name and patronymic and ἀντίον ηὔδα. As narration it carries no mark and no quotation mark; both begin with the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον, εἰ δ’ ἄγε νῦν μαντεύεο σοῖσι τέκεσσιν
οἴκαδ’ ἰών, μή πού τι κακὸν πάσχωσιν ὀπίσσω·
sentences.l:
“Old man, come now, go home and prophesy
to your own children, lest somehow they suffer some evil hereafter;
sentences.i: “Old man, why not go home and prophesy to your own children instead, in case they come to some harm later on;
sentences.n: This unit opens Eurymachus's speech, marked and quoted here rather than on the reply-formula line, as with Telemachus's speech above. εἰ δ’ ἄγε is a variant of the more usual ἀλλ’ ἄγε, both meaning 'come now'. μαντεύεο, present imperative, is contemptuous, telling Halitherses to practise his art where it is wanted, on his own family; μή … πάσχωσιν is a negative purpose clause. ὄπίσσω 'hereafter' is a common Homeric adverb of the future. γέρον is the vocative already fixed in the house table as 'Old man'.

sentences.t: ταῦτα δ’ ἐγὼ σέο πολλὸν ἀμείνων μαντεύεσθαι.
sentences.l: But in these things I am far better than you at prophesying.
sentences.i: But when it comes to this, I am a far better prophet than you.
sentences.n: σέο is the uncontracted genitive of comparison after ἀμείνων (Attic σοῦ); πολλόν is an adverbial accusative, 'by much, far'. Eurymachus claims superior insight while offering none, sheer bluster rather than argument.

sentences.t:
ὄρνιθες δέ τε πολλοὶ ὑπ’ αὐγὰς ἠελίοιο
φοιτῶσ’, οὐδέ τε πάντες ἐναίσιμοι·
sentences.l:
And many birds, under the rays of the sun,
go to and fro, and not all are true-omened;
sentences.i: Birds in plenty fly about under the light of the sun, and not all of them are omens that mean anything;
sentences.n: The epic τε in δέ τε (181) and οὐδέ τε (182) marks a general, standing truth, as first noted in the pilot; Eurymachus generalizes in order to dismiss the eagle-sign as mere chance. ἐναίσιμος, 'in keeping with what is due', describes a bird-sign as a true portent, the same word Halitherses used of his own skill at 2.159.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ὤλετο τῆλ’, ὡς καὶ σὺ καταφθίσθαι σὺν ἐκείνῳ
ὤφελες.
sentences.l:
but Odysseus
has perished far away, and I wish that you too, along with him,
had perished.
sentences.i: but Odysseus has died far from home — and I wish that you too had died along with him,
sentences.n: ὤφελες with an infinitive is the standard idiom for an unfulfilled wish about the past, 'you ought to have…', here bitterly, 'I wish you had died too'. ὤλετο is the intransitive aorist middle of ὄλλυμι, 'perished', matched by καταφθίσθαι, a stronger compound of the same idea. Eurymachus's wish runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἂν τόσσα θεοπροπέων ἀγόρευες,
οὐδέ κε Τηλέμαχον κεχολωμένον ὧδ’ ἀνιείης,
σῷ οἴκῳ δῶρον ποτιδέγμενος, αἴ κε πόρῃσιν.
sentences.l:
then you would not be speaking out so many prophecies,
nor would you be inciting Telemachus, angered as he is, in this way,
waiting for a gift for your household, in case he gives one.
sentences.i: then you would not be uttering so many prophecies, nor would you be egging Telemachus on in his anger like this, hoping for a gift for your house, in case he gives you one.
sentences.n: ἀγόρευες, imperfect indicative, and ἀνιείης, present optative, are both governed by ἄν/κε as the unreal apodosis begun with ὤφελες's wish; Homer can mix indicative and optative with ἄν in this way. κεχολωμένον is a perfect passive participle, 'in a state of anger'. Eurymachus accuses Halitherses of self-interest, hinting that his 'prophecies' aim at a reward from the anxious young Telemachus.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔκ τοι ἐρέω, τὸ δὲ καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.l: But I will speak out plainly to you, and this too shall be a thing fulfilled;
sentences.i: But I will tell you plainly, and this too will come true:
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἔκ … ἐρέω is tmesis for ἐξερέω, 'speak out, declare openly'. τετελεσμένον ἔσται is a periphrastic future perfect, 'will stand fulfilled', an emphatic assertion of certainty; Eurymachus borrows the very vocabulary of fulfilment (τελ-) that Halitherses has just used, and turns it into a threat of his own.

sentences.t:
αἴ κε νεώτερον ἄνδρα παλαιά τε πολλά τε εἰδὼς
παρφάμενος ἐπέεσσιν ἐποτρύνῃς χαλεπαίνειν,
αὐτῷ μέν οἱ πρῶτον ἀνιηρέστερον ἔσται,
πρῆξαι δ’ ἔμπης οὔ τι δυνήσεται εἵνεκα τῶνδε·
sentences.i: if, with all your old man's knowledge, you talk a younger man round and stir him up to anger, it will go the worse for him first of all, and even so he will be able to do nothing about any of this;
sentences.n: παλαιά … εἰδώς, 'knowing many old things', is a pointed jab at Halitherses' age, playing against ὦ γέρον at the speech's opening. παρφάμενος, from παράφημι, is 'talk someone round, beguile with words'; ἐποτρύνῃς χαλεπαίνειν governs an infinitive of what the younger man is incited to do. τῶνδε, 'because of these', points to the suitors present, whose numbers and resolve Eurymachus is confident Telemachus cannot overcome.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δέ, γέρον, θωὴν ἐπιθήσομεν, ἥν κ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
τίνων ἀσχάλλῃς·
sentences.l:
But on you, old man, we will lay a fine, which, paying it,
you will chafe at in your heart;
sentences.i: But on you, old man, we will impose a fine, one that will gall you at heart to pay;
sentences.n: γέρον again, kept 'old man' as at 2.178. θωή, 'a fine, penalty', is an unusual Homeric word for a monetary punishment; τίνων is the present participle of τίνω 'pay', and the relative clause with κ’ is a general future condition, 'one you will resent whenever you pay it'.

sentences.t: χαλεπὸν δέ τοι ἔσσεται ἄλγος.
sentences.l: and grievous will the pain be for you.
sentences.i: and it will be a painful thing for you.
sentences.n: ἄλγος 'pain, suffering' closes the threat against Halitherses begun in the unit before (2.192); χαλεπόν picks up χαλεπαίνειν from 2.189, tying this threat back to the one just made about Telemachus.

sentences.t: Τηλεμάχῳ δ’ ἐν πᾶσιν ἐγὼν ὑποθήσομαι αὐτός·
sentences.l: and to Telemachus, before you all, I myself will give counsel:
sentences.i: And to Telemachus, in front of you all, I myself will offer this advice:
sentences.n: ὑποτίθεμαι, 'lay down as a suggestion, advise', is a milder word than the commands Eurymachus has just been using; ἐν πᾶσιν, 'among/before all', stages the advice as a public pronouncement to the whole assembly, not a private word.

sentences.t: μητέρα ἣν ἐς πατρὸς ἀνωγέτω ἀπονέεσθαι·
sentences.l: let him bid his own mother go back to her father's house;
sentences.i: let him order his own mother to go back to her father's house;
sentences.n: ἣν is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν again, 'his own [mother]'. ἐς πατρός is a common Homeric idiom, 'to [the house] of her father', with the noun for 'house' left unexpressed. ἀνωγέτω is the same defective verb, ἄνωγα, as ἄνωχθι at 2.113, here a third-person imperative.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ γάμον τεύξουσι καὶ ἀρτυνέουσιν ἔεδνα
πολλὰ μάλ’, ὅσσα ἔοικε φίλης ἐπὶ παιδὸς ἕπεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and they will make ready the marriage and prepare the wedding-gifts,
very many, as many as is fitting to go with a dear daughter.
sentences.i: and they will arrange the marriage and prepare wedding gifts in great number, as many as it is fitting should go with a dear daughter.
sentences.n: This unit reuses, verbatim, its earlier appearance in odyssey-003 (1.277). οἱ δέ, 'her people', refers to Icarius's household; ἔεδνα are wedding gifts whose exact direction — from the suitor to the bride's family, or the reverse — has long been disputed and is not settled here, as already noted at 1.277 (odyssey-003) and 2.52–54 (odyssey-005).

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ πρὶν παύσεσθαι ὀίομαι υἷας Ἀχαιῶν
μνηστύος ἀργαλέης, ἐπεὶ οὔ τινα δείδιμεν ἔμπης,
sentences.l:
for I do not think the sons of the Achaeans will cease before then
from grievous wooing, since we fear no one at all, in any case,
sentences.i: for I do not believe the sons of the Achaeans will give up this grievous wooing before that, since in any case we fear no one,
sentences.n: μνηστύς ἀργαλέη, 'grievous wooing', is an abstract noun from the same root as μνηστῆρες 'suitors' and μνάομαι 'woo'; its rendering is fixed in new-renderings.md, as is the periphrasis υἷας Ἀχαιῶν already met at 2.115. δείδιμεν is a first plural perfect-with-present-sense of δείδω, 'we fear'.

sentences.t:
οὔτ’ οὖν Τηλέμαχον μάλα περ πολύμυθον ἐόντα,
οὔτε θεοπροπίης ἐμπαζόμεθ’, ἣν σύ, γεραιέ,
μυθέαι ἀκράαντον, ἀπεχθάνεαι δ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον.
sentences.l:
neither Telemachus, full of words though he very much is,
nor do we heed the prophecy, which you, old man,
speak in vain, and you grow only more hated for it.
sentences.i: neither Telemachus, talkative as he is, nor do we heed the prophecy that you, old man, speak so uselessly — and you only make yourself more hateful by it.
sentences.n: πολύμυθος, 'full of words, talkative', is a one-off jibe at Telemachus rather than a fixed epithet. γεραιέ is a second word for 'old man', from γεραιός rather than γέρων, the word behind ὦ γέρον earlier in this speech; it is kept to the same English rendering. ἀκράαντον, 'unaccomplished', is built with alpha-privative on the root of κραίνω, directly denying the τετελεσμένον Eurymachus himself claimed for his own words at 2.187. ἀπεχθάνομαι, 'become hateful', is almost a taunt: the more Halitherses prophesies, the less he will be liked for it.

sentences.t:
χρήματα δ’ αὖτε κακῶς βεβρώσεται, οὐδέ ποτ’ ἶσα
ἔσσεται, ὄφρα κεν ἥ γε διατρίβῃσιν Ἀχαιοὺς
ὃν γάμον·
sentences.i: and meanwhile his property will go on being shamefully eaten up, and it can never be made good again, for as long as she keeps the Achaeans waiting over her marriage;
sentences.n: βεβρώσεται is a future perfect passive of βιβρώσκω 'devour', emphasizing a completed state of loss rather than an ongoing one; ἶσα 'equal, even' implies the loss can never be made good again. ὅν γάμον is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν once more, 'her own marriage', with διατρίβῃσιν, 'wears out the time over', taking Ἀχαιούς as a kind of accusative of the persons kept waiting.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ αὖ ποτιδέγμενοι ἤματα πάντα
εἵνεκα τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐριδαίνομεν, οὐδὲ μετ’ ἄλλας
ἐρχόμεθ’, ἃς ἐπιεικὲς ὀπυιέμεν ἐστὶν ἑκάστῳ.
sentences.l:
but we, in turn, waiting all our days,
vie with one another for her excellence, and do not go after other women,
whom it would be fitting for each of us to marry.
sentences.i: but we, for our part, go on waiting day after day, competing for her excellence, and we do not go after other women, any of whom it would be quite proper for each of us to marry.
sentences.n: ἀρετή, 'excellence, worth', applied to a woman is her outstanding quality generally, not a single virtue. ἐριδαίνομεν is built on the same root as ἐριδαίνεμεν, the infinitive already noted in the pilot (1.78–79). ὀπυίω, 'take to wife, marry', is a synonym of γαμέω used only of the man. Eurymachus's speech is left open here: it runs on without a break into the next part, and the closing ” is not given.
